```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 15_related_anova_partitioning_variance
title: Where does it go?
questions:
  - id: slowest_person_shift
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      In a related-samples study, we take the participant who is already the
      slowest overall and add 10 seconds to all of their scores. Which of these
      sums of squares changes?
    options:
      - text: The between-groups sum of squares
      - text: The between-people sum of squares
        correct: true
      - text: The error sum of squares
    hint: >
      Does this person's pattern across the conditions change, or only their
      overall level?
    explanation: >
      This person's mean moves farther from the grand mean, so the
      between-people sum of squares grows. Every condition mean rises by
      the same amount, so the differences among conditions don't change. And
      the person's scores all move together, so nothing changes about how they
      respond to the conditions relative to everyone else. A person's overall
      level ends up entirely in the between-people component, which is
      why it can be taken out of the denominator. (The within-groups and total
      sums of squares grow too, since the between-people component is part of
      both.)

  - id: unusual_response
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Most participants score about 5 points higher in condition B than in
      condition A, but one participant scores 5 points lower. Which component
      does that participant's unusual response contribute to?
    options:
      - text: The between-people sum of squares
      - text: The error sum of squares
        correct: true
      - text: Neither; it is removed by the related-samples design
    explanation: >
      The related-samples design only removes a person's overall level. People
      responding differently to the conditions is left over, and so it ends up
      in the error component. That's why "error" here means more than
      sampling error, strictly defined.

  - id: gap_from_own_mean
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Stephen's time on the first race alone, 51 seconds, is 3 seconds above
      Stephen's own average across the three conditions. Which components can
      that gap contribute to?
    options:
      - text: The between-people and error sums of squares
      - text: The between-groups and error sums of squares
        correct: true
      - text: The between-people and between-groups sums of squares
    hint: >
      The gap compares one child with that same child. Could it say anything
      about how that child compares with other children?
    explanation: >
      The gap is measured from Stephen's own mean, so Stephen's overall level is
      already out of it, and it can't contribute to the between-people
      component. The first-alone mean sits 3.53 seconds above the grand mean:
      the between-groups part. Stephen's gap is 0.53 seconds smaller than that,
      so the error part is $-0.53$ seconds. Careful with the word "within" here: variability within a
      person and variability within a group are different things. Within a
      group, different children's scores vary, so that's where the people
      component comes from.
```
